acceptable.choice: Keep Laravel Reverb and scale it out: enable Reverb's Redis-backed horizontal scaling, run several Reverb processes per VM (one per core, since each process is single-threaded), and spread them behind the load balancer
acceptable.why: Reverb is built to scale this way, 60,000 connections is a modest number for a tuned cluster of event-loop servers, and nothing in the 300k-line app or the client code has to change.

acceptable.choice: Tune Reverb and the host before adding hardware: use the ext-uv (or ext-event) event loop instead of stream_select, raise file-descriptor and kernel socket limits, fix load-balancer WebSocket idle timeouts, and review activity timeout, max message size, Pulse/telemetry ingestion and debug settings
acceptable.why: The default PHP loop and OS limits often cause slow delivery and memory pressure at peak, and fixing them is cheap, quick and needs only skills the team already has.

acceptable.choice: Profile the whole broadcast path first (event dispatch, queue workers, Redis pub/sub, the Reverb event loop, client fan-out), then fix the actual bottleneck
acceptable.why: Slow delivery may come from queued broadcasts, too few queue workers, Redis, MySQL writes or presence-channel fan-out rather than the WebSocket server, and a Go rewrite would fix none of those.

acceptable.choice: Reduce per-connection and per-message cost: avoid presence channels with many members, trim payloads, use ShouldBroadcastNow or dedicated broadcast queues where it makes sense, and cut redundant channel subscriptions
acceptable.why: Fan-out and presence membership updates often dominate CPU and memory, so shrinking them pays off at 7.5x the load whatever server is used.

acceptable.choice: Load-test to about 1.5x the 60,000 target (roughly 90,000 connections at realistic message rates) with k6, Artillery or a Pusher-protocol load tool, including node-failure and reconnect-storm scenarios
acceptable.why: This is the only way to know the needed node count and cost, and to have proof before the customer arrives.

acceptable.choice: Larger or memory-optimised VMs for the Reverb tier as a stopgap
acceptable.why: This buys headroom within days at a known cost while the measuring and tuning happen.

acceptable.choice: Soketi (a self-hosted, Pusher-protocol-compatible server) as a fallback if tuned Reverb can't meet the per-node cost target
acceptable.why: It is a drop-in swap at the protocol level with no client or backend rewrite, but its slower maintenance pace should be checked first.

acceptable.choice: Managed Pusher-compatible service (Pusher Channels, Ably) as an emergency bridge or overflow for the big customer
acceptable.why: It is a configuration-level switch that removes operational risk before the deadline, but at 60,000 connections it is likely far more expensive than self-hosting, so it must be priced against the hosting-cost priority.

acceptable.choice: Isolate the large customer on its own Reverb app or node pool
acceptable.why: This limits blast radius for reliability and makes their load easy to measure and to bill against.

acceptable.choice: A Go realtime service (custom Pusher-protocol-compatible, or Centrifugo) as a later, evidence-driven project after the launch
acceptable.why: It is reasonable only if measurements show Reverb's cost per connection stays unacceptable after tuning, and only when there is time to staff it beyond two people.

ruled_out.choice: Rewriting the realtime layer in Go before the big customer arrives
ruled_out.why: It puts a 3-month hard deadline at risk on a from-scratch rewrite by 2 of 12 engineers (bus factor, ops and on-call knowledge), and it does nothing for the bottlenecks that are likely outside the socket server.

ruled_out.choice: Switching to a non-Pusher protocol (Centrifugo, a custom Go or Node protocol, Socket.IO) inside the 3-month window
ruled_out.why: It needs client SDK, channel-auth and backend broadcasting changes across a large app, plus a migration, all under a deadline with paying customers.

ruled_out.choice: Rewriting in Elixir/Phoenix, Node, Rust or another stack the team doesn't know
ruled_out.why: Nobody on the team has the skills, the deadline is close, and running two stacks long-term costs more.

ruled_out.choice: Rewriting or splitting the Laravel monolith into microservices to fix this
ruled_out.why: It is far out of scope and adds no realtime capacity in time.

ruled_out.choice: Migrating to Kubernetes or a new platform as part of this fix
ruled_out.why: It changes the deploy and ops model under deadline pressure without fixing the bottleneck, and the team runs plain VMs today.

ruled_out.choice: Only adding more of today's Reverb VMs without enabling Redis scaling or tuning
ruled_out.why: Without Redis scaling, messages don't reach clients on other nodes, and scaling an untuned setup 7.5x multiplies hosting cost.

must_mention: Don't do the Go rewrite before the deadline: 3 months with 2 Go engineers is too risky for a launch with paying customers, and a rewrite can wait until measurements justify it
Measure first: find out whether the memory and latency problems are in Reverb itself or in queues, Redis, the database or broadcast fan-out
Reverb scales horizontally through Redis pub/sub across several processes and nodes behind the load balancer, and each process is single-threaded, so run several per VM
Practical Reverb tuning: the ext-uv/ext-event loop (stream_select limits connections to about 1,024), file-descriptor and kernel limits, load-balancer WebSocket timeouts
Load-test above 60,000 connections with realistic message rates before the customer goes live
Reliability under failure: N+1 capacity so a dead node's connections can reconnect elsewhere, client reconnect with jitter and backoff, and graceful draining during deploys
Keeping the Pusher protocol means Soketi or a managed service stays a low-risk fallback
Estimate the hosting cost of the scaled setup (node count times VM price) and weigh it against managed-service pricing
Rough capacity maths: estimate memory per connection from today's numbers, then project to 60,000 plus headroom
red_flags: Recommending the Go rewrite as the main plan before the deadline, or claiming Go is needed to handle 60,000 connections
Assuming the WebSocket server is the bottleneck without asking for profiling or metrics
Treating 60,000 concurrent connections as extreme scale that needs exotic technology
Saying PHP or Reverb can't handle this load without mentioning Redis scaling, multiple processes or event-loop tuning
Recommending a protocol change or migration that touches client SDKs and auth across a 300k-line app within 3 months
Recommending managed Pusher or Ably without pointing out the significant cost at 60,000 connections when hosting cost is a stated priority
Ignoring failure modes: reconnect storms, load-balancer limits, deploy disconnects, single points of failure in Redis
Giving no load-testing or validation plan before a contractual go-live
Making two engineers the only owners of a critical new service without addressing the bus-factor and on-call risk
Quoting made-up benchmark numbers as if they were facts about this system
unknowns: Where the delivery latency actually comes from: Reverb's event loop, queue workers, Redis, the database or the client
Memory per connection today, and whether the memory grows (leak) or stays flat
Which event loop Reverb uses now, the Reverb version, and whether Redis scaling is already on
How many of the 10 VMs run Reverb, and their sizes
Message rate per chat and fan-out per message (channels per chat, presence-channel sizes, agents watching many chats)
How the big customer's traffic behaves: a gradual ramp or a big-bang cutover, peak shape, any SLA or latency terms in the contract
Load-balancer type and its WebSocket connection and timeout limits
Redis capacity and topology (single instance or HA) under 7.5x pub/sub load
Budget limits and whether paying for a managed service is acceptable
Whether the Go engineers' proposal rests on measured Reverb limits or on assumptions
